title: Noncompete Agreements, Come On
summary: Josh and Chuck explain non-compete agreements (NCAs): what they are, why employers use them (protecting trade secrets, recouping training investment, keeping client bases), and why critics call them unfair. They trace the history from the 1414 Dyer's case and the 1711 Mitchell v. Reynolds baker case in England, through freedom of contract in the mid-1800s, Reconstruction-era concerns about wage slavery, and California's 1872 ban. They cover modern statistics (about one in five private-sector workers under an NCA), abuses like the Jimmy John's case and no-poach agreements, the Oregon 2008 ban and its wage effects, FTC estimates of economic gains, Massachusetts's 2018 ban, arguments from the US Chamber of Commerce, workarounds like NDAs and non-solicitation agreements, garden leave, and the FTC's January 2023 proposal to ban non-competes with public comments due March 20. The episode closes with a listener mail from Heather and Ronan.

segments.title: Opening banter and noncompete overview
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, then introduce non-compete agreements as a topic, arguing they hurt competition and that about one in five Americans work under one.

segments.title: What non-competes are and why companies use them
segments.summary: They describe typical non-compete terms (time limits, geographic limits, sale of a business) and the three commonly accepted justifications: protecting trade secrets, recouping training investment, and keeping client bases. They note that the client-base use is the one they object to most, citing hairstylists and dog groomers.

segments.title: Arguments for and against non-competes
segments.summary: They present the argument that without non-competes companies would invest less in employees, and compare employment to a broken relationship to show the inherent unfairness.

segments.title: Early English history: Dyer's case and Mitchell v. Reynolds
segments.summary: The hosts trace non-competes to fifteenth and sixteenth century English guilds. They describe the 1414 Dyer's case, where courts sided with an apprentice dyer against a six-month London ban, and the 1711 Mitchell v. Reynolds case, where a baker who leased his bakery and promised not to compete was held to his agreement because the parties were on equal footing.

segments.title: Freedom of contract, Reconstruction, and wage slavery
segments.summary: Courts shifted toward employers in the mid-1800s with freedom of contract. Aisha Bell Hardaway's scholarship links US protections against predatory contracts to Reconstruction-era Black Codes and the Thirteenth Amendment. The hosts discuss wage dependence and the imbalance of power.

segments.title: California's 1872 ban and enforceability
segments.summary: They note California banned non-competes in 1872, and that the states largely set their own rules. They explain that a contract's unenforceability depends on the state, and that high-skilled workers with access to trade secrets usually lose these cases.

segments.title: Modern prevalence and low-wage workers
segments.summary: They cite economist Evans Starr's research showing about twenty percent of private-sector workers are under a non-compete, with many low-wage and food service workers. They explain that lower-wage workers typically get no real consideration beyond keeping their job.

segments.title: Jimmy John's, no-poach agreements, and state investigations
segments.summary: They discuss reports that Jimmy John's required sandwich workers to sign non-competes, which the company dropped after a state attorney general investigation. They also describe no-poach agreements between franchises and their subsequent dropping after state investigations.

segments.title: Oregon ban, FTC economic estimates, and doctors
segments.summary: They cite Oregon's 2008 partial ban, which an FTC study found raised hourly wages by two to three percent statewide, with a fourteen to twenty-one percent increase for workers previously under non-competes. They also cite FTC estimates of job creation and wage gains, healthcare savings from eliminating doctor non-competes, and Massachusetts's 2018 ban.

segments.title: Arguments for non-competes, workarounds, and the FTC proposal
segments.summary: They cover the US Chamber of Commerce's defense of non-competes and the counterarguments, then describe workarounds such as NDAs, IP agreements, non-solicitation agreements, and garden leave. They conclude with the FTC's January 2023 proposal to ban non-competes, with public comments due March 20, and possible Congressional action.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh reads a listener mail from Heather about discovering the show during the spring of 2020 and listening with her son Ronan. They close with contact information.
